    #Tutorial 1 (Crystallographic Directions & Planes)

    #Question 1

    What are some important properties of each engineering material?

    • Metallic materials
    • Polymeric materials
    • Ceramic materials
    • Smart materials
    Metals- High strength
    - Excellent conductors of electricity and heat
    - Ferrous materials have desirable magnetic properties
    Polymers- Extremely ductile and pliable (easily form into any shape)
    - Low densities (lightweight)
    - Some are transparent
    - Chemically inert
    Ceramics- High strength but brittle
    - Insulators to electricity and heat
    - Some have useful high temperature strength
    Smart Materials- Able to sense and respond to environmental changes
    - Temperature, electric potential, magnetic field, light, etc.

    An example of a smart material is piezoelectric ceramics, which expand and contract
    in response to an applied electric field (voltage). Conversely, they also generate an
    electric field when they are deformed.

    mCu​=0.8 g

    mNi​=0.2 g

    Atomic masses of Cu and Ni,

    Cu=63.546 g/mol

    Ni=58.693 g/mol

    Mass of a Cu atom,

    mCu​=6.022×102363.546​

    mCu​=1.0552×10−22 g/atom

    Number of Cu atoms,

    xCu​=1.0552×10−220.8​

    xCu​=7.5815×1021 atoms

    Atomic percentage of Cu,

    %Cu=7.5815+2.05207.5815​

    %Cu=78.7%

    Mass of a Ni atom,

    mNi​=6.022×102258.693​

    mNi​=9.7464×10−23 g/atom

    Number of Ni atoms,

    xNi​=9.7464×10−230.2​

    xNi​=2.0520×1021 atoms

    Atomic percentage of Ni,

    %Ni=7.5815+2.05202.0520​

    %Ni=21.3%

    Direction in the 3-axis system,

    A=[1ˉ01]

    B=[111]

    In the 3-axis system, direction is represented by [U,V,W].
    In the 4-axis system, direction is represented by     [u,v,t,w].

    Converting A to the 4-axis system,

    u=32U−V​=32(−1)−0​=−32​

    v=32V−U​=32(0)−(−1)​=31​

    t=−3U+V​=−3−1+0​=31​

    w=W=1

    Converting B to the 4-axis system,

    u=32U−V​=32(1)−1​=31​

    v=32V−U​=32(1)−1​=31​

    t=−3U+V​=−31+1​=−32​

    w=W=1

    Direction in the 4-axis system,

    A=[2ˉ113]

    B=[112ˉ3]

    Multiply the indices by 3 to express them as whole numbers.

    #Part (b)

    B=[211]

    In the 3-axis system, direction is represented by [U,V,W].

    u=32U−V​=32(−1)−1​=−1

    #Question 5

    • Minimum shear stress required to initiate the slip process
    • Stress value is essentially the yield stress of a single crystal
    • Once critical shear stress is reached on a specific atomic plane, the top half
      plane will slip on the bottom half plane in the direction of the shear stress
    • Excessive slip will result in fracture of the single crystal along the slip plane

    #Question 3

    Fine pearlite and pro-eutectoid ferrite:

    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → ferrite region
    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → pearlite region
    • Cut lower section of austenite → pearlite region to obtain fine pearlite

    Martensite:

    • Cut the start line of austenite → martensite region
    • Does not cut any other transformation regions

    Martensite and pro-eutectoid ferrite:

    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → ferrite region
    • Cut the start line of austenite → martensite region

    Coarse pearlite and pro-eutectoid ferrite:

    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → ferrite region
    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → pearlite region
    • Cut upper section of austenite → pearlite region to obtain coarse pearlite

    Martensite, fine pearlite, and pro-eutectoid ferrite:

    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → ferrite region
    • Cut both the start and end lines of austenite → pearlite region
    • Cut lower section of austenite → pearlite region to obtain fine pearlite

    #Question 4

    • Insufficient activation energy due to low ageing temperature
    • Solid solution must be heated to a sufficiently high ageing temperature and held at
      that temperature for an adequate duration to achieve the required activation energy

    #Question 5

    Effects of recovery:

    • Internal residual stress (strain energy) is greatly reduced
    • Slight decrease in both strength and hardness
    • Significant increase in ductility of recovered metal

    Effects of recrystallization:

    • Internal residual stress (strain energy) is reduced further
    • Significant decrease in both strength and hardness
    • Significant increase in ductility of recovered metal

    #Tutorial 5 (Engineering Alloys)

    #Question 1

    Al2024-T4 and Al2024-T6 are heat treatable alloys.
    Sketch the processes in which they are heat treated.
    What is the major difference in properties? Explain.

    TemperHeat Treatment Process
    T4Solution-treated and naturally aged
    T6Solution-treated and artificially aged

    Artificial ageing results in the formation of finely dispersed precipitates,
    which strengthens the alloy. Al2024-T6 will be stronger than Al2024-T4.

    #Question 2

    Would you expect a Al2024-T9 aluminum alloy to be
    stronger or weaker than an Al2024-T6 alloy? Explain.

    TemperHeat Treatment Process
    T6Solution-treated and artificially aged
    T9Solution-treated, artificially aged, and cold-worked

    Cold-worked further strengthens the alloy via strain hardening.
    Thus, Al2024-T9 will be stronger than Al2024-T6.

    #Question 3

    Quenching (low alloy content):

    • β phase transforms to α′ titanium martensite when it crosses the Ms​ line
    • When reheated to temper temperature, β precipitates form from α′
    • Tempering process (decrease the strength of the alloy)
    • α′→α grains+β precipitates

    Quenching (high alloy content):

    • β phase transforms to supersaturated titanium βss​ when quenched
    • When reheated to temper temperature, α precipitates are formed
    • Age-hardening process (increase the strength of the alloy)
    • βss​→β grains+α precipitates

    #Question 4

    In what aspect are the nickel-based superalloys “super”?

    • High strength at elevated temperatures
    • High oxidation resistance (corrosion resistance)
    • Resistance to creep at elevated temperatures

    #Question 5

    Density of each material,

    ρAl​=2.7 g/cm3

    ρNi​=8.9 g/cm3

    ρNi3​Al​=7.5 g/cm3

    Atomic masses,

    MAl​=26.98 g/mol

    MNi​=58.7 g/mol

    Assume alloy has a mass of 100 g.

    mAl​=5 g

    mNi​=95 g

    Volume percent of precipitate,

    %V=VNi​+VNi3​Al​VNi3​Al​​

    %V=mNi​/ρNi​+mNi3​Al​/ρNi3​Al​mNi3​Al​/ρNi3​Al​​

    Note that the alloy’s microstructure consists of a
    nickel matrix with nickel-aluminum precipitates.

    Number of Al atoms,

    nAl​=MAl​mAl​​NA​

    nAl​=26.985NA​​

    nAl​=0.18532NA​

    where NA​ is Avogadro’s number

    Number of Ni atoms,

    nNi​=MNi​mNi​​NA​

    nNi​=58.795NA​​

    nNi​=1.6184NA​

    where NA​ is Avogadro’s number

    Number of Ni atoms that react with Al atoms,

    nNi,react​=3nAl​=3(0.18532NA​)=0.55597NA​

    Remaining number of Ni atoms,

    nNi,remain​=1.6184NA​−0.55597NA​=1.0624NA​

    Mass of precipitate,

    mNi3​Al​=NA​nAl​​MAl​+NA​nNireact​​​MNi​

    mNi3​Al​=NA​0.18532NA​(26.98)​+NA​0.55597NA​(58.7)​

    mNi3​Al​=37.635 g

    Mass of remaining nickel,

    mNi​=NA​nNi,remain​​MNi​

    mNi​=NA​1.0624NA​(58.7)​

    mNi​=62.365 g

    Volume percent of precipitate,

    %V=mNi​/ρNi​+mNi3​Al​/ρNi3​Al​mNi3​Al​/ρNi3​Al​​

    %V=(62.365/8.9)+(37.635/7.5)37.635/7.5​

    %V=41.729%

    #Tutorial 6 (Composite Materials)

    #Question 1

    Describe the various classes of composites based on:

    • Type of reinforcement used
    • Type of reinforcement materials
    • Type of matrix used
    • Reinforcement orientation and stacking sequence adopted

    Types of reinforcement used:

    • Continuous fibers — long fibers that are oriented in one or more directions
    • Short fibers (whiskers) — fibers are randomly oriented
    • Particulate — in the form of particles

    Types of reinforcement material:

    • Carbon fiber reinforced
    • Glass fiber reinforced
    • Kevlar (aramid) fiber reinforced

    Types of matrix used:

    • Polymer matrix composite
    • Metal matrix composite
    • Ceramic matrix composite

    Reinforcement orientation:

    • Unidirectional — continuous fibers that are aligned in a single direction
    • Bi-directional — continuous fibers that are aligned in 2 directions
    • 3D composite — continuous fibers that are aligned in 3 directions
    • Isotropic — short fibers that are randomly oriented

    Stacking sequence:

    • Quasi-isotropic — plies are arranged such that properties are nearly the same
      in all directions (composite material behaves as a near-isotropic material)
    • Angle-ply — plies are arranged at angles corresponding to loading directions
    • Symmetric — plies are arranged symmetrical about mid-plane of the laminate

    #Question 2

    Maximum load supported by fiber,

    Ff​=σf​Af​

    Ff​=σf​(4πd2​)

    Shear force at matrix/fiber interface,

    Ff​=τm​A

    Ff​=τm​(πd⋅2lcr​​)

    Equating the above,

    σf​(4πd2​)=τm​(πd⋅2lcr​​)

    lcr​=d(2τm​σf​​)

    where σf​ is the failure stress of the fiber,
    and     τm​ is the matrix shear strength

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Longitudinal direction (isostrain),

    Ec​=Ef​Vf​+Em​Vm​

    145=Ef​(0.6)+Em​(1−0.6)

    145=0.6Ef​+0.4Em​

    Ef​=3725​−32​Em​

    Transverse direction (isostress),

    Ec​=Vf​Em​+Vm​Ef​Ef​Em​​

    9.4=0.6Em​+0.4Ef​Ef​Em​​

    Ef​Em​=5.64Em​+3.76Ef​

    Substituting Ef​ into the isostrain equation,

    (3725​−32​Em​)Em​=5.64Em​+3.76(3725​−32​Em​)

    3725​Em​−32​Em​2=5.64Em​+32726​−75188​Em​

    0=32​Em​2−153578​Em​+32726​

    Solving the quadratic equation,

    Em​=353.95 GPa or Em​=3.8508 GPa

    Ef​=5.7 GPa or Ef​=239.10 GPa

    Since fibers are typically the stronger material,

    Em​=3.8508 GPa

    Ef​=239.10 GPa

    εc​=εm​=εf​

    Ec​εc​Ac​=Em​εm​Am​+Ef​εf​Af​

    Ec​Ac​=Em​Am​+Ef​Af​

    Both matrix and fibers have the same length.

    Ec​Vc​=Em​Vm​+Ef​Vf​     −[2]

    Comparing [1] and [2],

    Pc​Pf​​=Em​Vm​+Ef​Vf​Ef​Vf​​

    #Question 4

    Particle density measures:

    • True density — density of the metal if the powders were melted into a solid mass
    • Bulk density — density of the powders in the loose state after pouring

    Deep drawing:

    • Cold sheetmetal forming process (to fabricate cup-shaped parts)
    • Sheetmetal blank is forced into a die cavity by mechanical action of a punch
    • Process is considered “deep” when depth of drawn part exceeds its diameter
    • Deep drawing materials are easily shapeable materials due to their high ductility

    Wire/bar drawing:

    • Workpiece in the form of a cylindrical bar is pulled through a converging die
    • Metal is squeezed down as it passes through the die opening
    • Cross-section area of the workpiece is reduced

    Advantages of cold working:

    • Higher strength and hardness due to strain hardening
    • Directional properties due to grain flow
    • No heating of workpiece is required
    • Better surface finish and accuracy

    #Question 5

    Packing factor of metal powder,

    PF=ρtrue​ρbulk​​=m/Vtrue​m/Vbulk​​=Vbulk​Vtrue​​

    Let the true volume be Vtrue​=1 m3.

    Bulk volume of metal powder,

    0.5=Vbulk​Vtrue​​

    Vbulk​=2

    Bulk volume after pressing and sintering,

    Vbulk​=0.9(32​×2)=1.2 m3

    Packing factor after pressing and sintering,

    PF=Vbulk​Vtrue​​=1.21​=0.833

    Final porosity,

    Porosity+Packing Factor=1

    Porosity=1−0.833=0.167
